description: Permanent term lookup. Read by web/app.js to surface instant definitions on highlight. Claude appends/updates entries when explaining terms in chat.

bond.definition: A loan with paperwork. You give a borrower money now and they promise to pay you a stream of interest payments plus the principal back at the end. The receipt is the bond.

stock.definition: A slice of ownership in a company. Unlike a bond (a loan), a stock makes you a part-owner; you don't get the money back, but you share in profits forever via dividends or capital gains.

equity.definition: Synonym for ownership in a company. 'Equity' is the conceptual word; 'stock' or 'share' is the receipt. Equity claims are residual — they get paid only after debt is paid.

treasury.definition: A bond issued by the US government. Considered the 'risk-free' asset because the US can print dollars to repay. Maturities run from 1 month to 30 years; their yields anchor every other rate in the dollar system.

10y treasury.definition: A US government bond with 10 years to maturity. The 'belly' of the curve — the most-watched single rate in the world. When people say 'the 10Y is at 4.30%', they mean its current yield.

30y treasury.definition: The longest commonly-issued US government bond. More sensitive to inflation and term-premium changes than shorter bonds because you're locked in for 30 years. Think of it as the long-duration end of the rate spectrum.

2y treasury.definition: A US government bond with 2 years to maturity. Tracks Fed expectations closely — when markets price more rate cuts, the 2Y falls; when markets price hikes or higher-for-longer, it rises.

yield.definition: The interest rate you earn on a bond, expressed as a percentage. If a $1000 bond pays $43 a year, its yield is 4.3%. Yields move *inversely* to bond prices — when prices rise, yields fall.

coupon.definition: The periodic interest payment a bond pays its holder, expressed as a percent of face value. A '5% coupon' bond pays $50/year on a $1000 face value. Distinct from *yield* (which depends on the price you paid).

yield curve.definition: The plot of bond yields by maturity. Normally upward-sloping (longer = more risk = higher yield). Its shape is a real-time poll on the economy: steep means growth optimism, flat means uncertainty, inverted means recession expected.

yield curve inversion.definition: When short-term yields exceed long-term yields — abnormal because you're paid less for locking up money longer. Happens because markets expect rate cuts soon (recession). Has preceded most US recessions.

bear-flattening.definition: Curve flattening driven by the *short end rising* (e.g., inflation expectations or hawkish Fed pushing 2Y yields up). The 'bear' part: rising yields are bad for bondholders. Distinct from bull-flattening (driven by long end falling on growth fears).

bull-flattening.definition: Curve flattening driven by the *long end falling* (e.g., 10Y yields drop on growth fears or recession expectations). The 'bull' part: falling yields are good for existing bondholders. Opposite driver of bear-flattening despite same shape.

duration.definition: How sensitive a bond's price is to a change in interest rates. A 30Y has high duration; a 2Y has low duration. By extension, 'long-duration assets' (tech stocks, real estate) get hit hardest when rates rise.

term premium.definition: The extra yield investors demand for holding longer-dated bonds, beyond just expected average short rates. It's the price of *not knowing* what'll happen over 10–30 years — inflation surprises, policy shocks, supply changes.

real yield.definition: Bond yield minus inflation expectations. The actual purchasing power growth your bond gives you. Nominal yield can be 4% but if inflation is 5%, real yield is -1% — you're losing real money.

nominal yield.definition: The headline interest rate on a bond, before adjusting for inflation. If a Treasury yields 4.30%, that's nominal. Doesn't tell you what your purchasing power actually grows by.

tips.definition: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities. Bonds whose principal adjusts with inflation, so they pay a *real* yield directly. Useful as the market's read on real interest rates separate from inflation.

breakevens.definition: Inflation breakevens = nominal Treasury yield minus TIPS yield. The market's implied inflation expectation over that maturity. If 10Y breakeven is 2.5%, the market thinks average inflation will run 2.5% over 10 years.

inflation compensation.definition: Same idea as breakevens — the part of nominal bond yields that's compensating you for expected inflation. When 'the 2Y rose on inflation compensation,' it means the rise was driven by inflation expectations, not real-rate changes.

credit spread.definition: The extra yield a corporate (or any non-government) bond pays above the equivalent Treasury, compensating for default risk. MSFT 10Y at 4.80% vs. Treasury 10Y at 4.30% = 50bp credit spread. Widens in stress, tightens in calm.

credit market.definition: The bond market, especially for non-government borrowers (corporates, financials, sovereigns ex-US). 'Credit' here just means 'debt/lending.' Investment grade (IG) and high yield (HY) are the two main tiers.

basis points.definition: A unit equal to 0.01% (one hundredth of a percentage point). 'Spreads widened by 50 bps' = spreads rose by 0.5 percentage points. Used because rate moves are often small in absolute terms.

discount rate.definition: The rate you use to value future cash flows in today's dollars. Roughly: real yield + risk premium for the asset. When real yields rise, discount rate rises, and *every long-duration asset gets cheaper* (tech stocks, real estate, bonds).

free cash flow.definition: FCF = cash from operations minus capex. The cash a company actually generates after maintaining itself. Negative FCF means the business is consuming cash; sustainable only with external funding (debt or equity issuance).

capex.definition: Capital expenditure. Money spent on long-lived physical assets — factories, machinery, GPUs, data centers, fiber. Distinct from OpEx (day-to-day costs). The 'AI capex cycle' is hyperscalers spending hundreds of billions on AI infrastructure.

opex.definition: Operating expenses. Day-to-day costs to run a business — salaries, electricity, rent. Recurring; appears on the income statement, not the balance sheet (unlike capex, which becomes a depreciable asset).

hyperscaler.definition: The handful of cloud-computing giants operating at planetary scale: Microsoft (Azure), Google (GCP), Amazon (AWS), Meta, and increasingly Oracle. Together they're spending ~$700B in 2026 capex, ~75% of which is AI-specific.

fed.definition: The Federal Reserve, the US central bank. Sets the federal funds rate (the overnight bank lending rate), which propagates through every other interest rate in the dollar system. The FOMC is its rate-setting committee.

fomc.definition: Federal Open Market Committee. The 12-member Fed body that sets the federal funds rate at 8 meetings per year. Its statements, press conferences, and minutes move bond markets globally.

sep.definition: Summary of Economic Projections. Quarterly forecasts each FOMC member submits — for GDP, inflation, unemployment, and the funds rate. The 'dot plot' showing each member's rate forecast comes from this.

dxy.definition: The US Dollar Index. A trade-weighted measure of the dollar against six major currencies (mostly EUR, JPY, GBP). DXY at 100 was a baseline; ~98.5 today means the dollar is slightly weaker than that benchmark.

reserve currency.definition: A currency that other countries hold as foreign-exchange reserves and use for international trade. The USD is the dominant reserve currency (~58% of allocated reserves), giving the US 'exorbitant privilege.'

exorbitant privilege.definition: Coined by French finance minister Giscard d'Estaing in 1965. Because the world demands USD reserves and Treasuries, the US can run persistent fiscal and trade deficits at lower borrowing costs than any other country.

triffin's dilemma.definition: The structural tension of being the world's reserve issuer: to supply enough USD globally, the US must run trade deficits (export dollars). But persistent deficits eventually erode confidence in the currency. Slow corrosion is the price of dominance.

petrodollar.definition: The system where oil-exporting countries get paid in USD and recycle those dollars into Treasuries — financing US deficits. Linked oil pricing to USD demand since the 1970s. Erosion of this would be a meaningful reserve-currency shift.

lpr.definition: Loan Prime Rate. China's main lending benchmark, set monthly by the PBOC based on quotes from major banks. It's the Chinese equivalent of the Fed funds rate as a transmission point — though China uses other tools more actively.

pboc.definition: People's Bank of China. China's central bank. Less independent than the Fed (operates within the State Council), but increasingly important as China's macro management has become more sophisticated.

balance sheet recession.definition: Richard Koo's framework: when the private sector is paying down debt after a bubble bursts, monetary stimulus fails because nobody wants to borrow at any rate. Japan post-1990; China post-2021 property unwind. Multi-decade workout, not cyclical.

deflation.definition: Sustained falling prices. Sounds harmless but is dangerous: consumers delay purchases (prices will be lower), firms cut wages, debt becomes harder to service in real terms. Hardest macro condition for central banks to fight.

ipo.definition: Initial Public Offering. A private company's first sale of stock to public investors, raising cash and creating a tradable share. After the IPO, the stock trades in the secondary market without affecting the company's cash directly.

primary market.definition: Where borrowers raise capital for the first time — IPOs, bond issuances. Cash flows from investors *to* the issuing company. Distinct from the secondary market where investors trade among themselves afterward.

secondary market.definition: Where investors trade existing stocks and bonds among themselves. The stock market you see on CNBC is mostly secondary — when you buy NVDA on Nasdaq, NVDA gets nothing; you're buying from another holder.

liquidity.definition: Two meanings: (1) how easily an asset can be sold without moving the price (a Treasury is liquid; a privately-held company is illiquid); (2) how much money is sloshing around in the financial system.

hbm.definition: High-Bandwidth Memory. A stack of DRAM chips bonded directly to a GPU's package, providing the massive memory bandwidth AI training needs. SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron are the suppliers; allocation is contested.

cowos.definition: Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate. TSMC's advanced packaging technology that integrates a GPU die with HBM stacks on a single substrate. Currently the binding bottleneck in AI silicon supply, more so than raw wafer capacity.

advanced packaging.definition: The post-fabrication step that combines multiple chips (logic + memory + interconnect) into a single integrated package. Has gone from afterthought to bottleneck as AI chips push the limits of what a single die can do.

ppa.definition: Power Purchase Agreement. A long-term contract where a buyer (e.g., Microsoft) agrees to buy electricity from a generator (e.g., a nuclear plant) at a fixed price for 10–20 years. Used by hyperscalers to lock in clean baseload power for AI data centers.

nuclear restart.definition: Bringing a previously-decommissioned US nuclear plant back online. Three Mile Island Unit 1 (MSFT PPA, 2024) and Palisades (Holtec) are the leading examples — driven by AI's need for clean baseload power that the grid can't supply otherwise.

baseload.definition: Continuous, always-on electricity generation — nuclear, geothermal, large hydro, some natural gas. Distinct from intermittent (solar, wind). AI data centers need 24/7 power, so they pay premium for baseload sources.

behind-the-meter.definition: Power generated on-site (e.g., a gas turbine next to a data center) instead of taken from the grid. Hyperscalers are increasingly building behind-the-meter because grid interconnection queues are 5+ years.

supercycle.definition: An extended period (5–15 years) of structurally higher commodity prices, driven by demand outpacing supply when supply is hard to bring online (mines take 10+ years). Current thesis: electrification + AI + reshoring meeting decade-long underinvestment.

scaling laws.definition: Empirical observation that AI model capability increases predictably with more compute, data, and parameters. Has held for 7+ years. The entire AI capex thesis depends on this curve continuing — a flagship release that breaks it would be the regime change.

post-zirp.definition: The era after Zero Interest-Rate Policy ended — i.e., post-2022, when the Fed lifted rates from ~0% back to a regular regime. ZIRP (2009–2022, with brief interruption) was the historic anomaly; 'post-ZIRP' just means rates and capital costs are no longer free, which has reshaped private credit, IPO conditions, and the cost of long-duration assets.

zirp.definition: Zero Interest-Rate Policy. The Fed (and most major central banks) held policy rates near 0% from 2009 to 2015, again from 2020 to 2022. Made capital effectively free, which inflated long-duration asset prices (tech stocks, real estate, growth equity) and birthed the 'free money' era of venture capital and SaaS.

smic.definition: Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation. China's largest domestic chip foundry, government-backed, tasked with achieving leading-edge manufacturing independence. Currently producing 7nm-class chips with reportedly poor yields using workarounds (multi-patterning on older DUV tools). Blocked from ASML's EUV machines by US export controls.

euv.definition: Extreme Ultraviolet lithography. ASML's chipmaking tool that uses 13.5nm light to pattern sub-7nm features; required for 5nm and below. ASML (Dutch) is the sole supplier globally. Export controls on EUV to China are the single most important hardware choke point in the US-China chip tech competition.

asml.definition: Dutch company and sole global supplier of EUV lithography machines. Without ASML, TSMC, Samsung, and Intel cannot manufacture leading-edge chips. The Dutch government, under US pressure, extended export controls to include ASML's older DUV machines as well, further restricting Chinese fab options.

process node.definition: The marketing term for a chip generation (7nm, 5nm, 3nm, 2nm). The number no longer literally means the transistor size but is a competitive benchmark. Each new node packs more transistors in the same area, improving performance and efficiency. TSMC and Samsung are at 3nm; Intel is catching up at 18A/20A.

tsmc.definition: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. The world's dominant chip foundry — makes chips for Apple, NVDA, AMD, Qualcomm, and most AI labs. Its concentration in Taiwan is the central geopolitical risk in the semiconductor supply chain.

export controls.definition: Government rules restricting which hardware and technology can be sold to which countries. The US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issues these. Key AI-relevant controls: H100/H200/B100 GPU exports to China; EUV machine exports; ASML DUV restrictions. Updated frequently — a new BIS rule can reshape the competitive landscape overnight.

bis.definition: Bureau of Industry and Security (US Commerce Dept). Issues export control rules that govern which technologies can be sold to which countries. For AI, BIS controls GPU exports, chip tool exports (EUV/DUV), and adds companies to the Entity List (effectively a sanctions-lite designation). One of the most consequential AI-policy actors.

entity list.definition: A BIS list of foreign companies and organizations that US exporters cannot sell to without a license (usually denied). SMIC, Huawei, and hundreds of Chinese AI and defense firms are on it. Being added to the Entity List is effectively a supply chain death sentence for hardware-dependent companies.

eu ai act.definition: The EU's comprehensive AI regulation, adopted 2024. Classifies AI systems by risk (unacceptable, high, limited, minimal). 'General Purpose AI' (GPAI) models above a compute threshold (~10²⁵ FLOPs) face transparency, evaluation, and incident-reporting obligations. Frontier GPAI models face stricter adversarial testing requirements.

gpai.definition: General Purpose AI Model. The EU AI Act's term for large foundation models (LLMs, multimodal models) that can be used for many downstream tasks. Above 10²⁵ FLOPs training compute: transparency and copyright obligations. 'Systemic risk' GPAI above 10²⁶ FLOPs: adversarial testing, incident reporting, model evaluation before deployment.

compute threshold.definition: A FLOPs (floating-point operations) cutoff used in regulation to define 'frontier' AI models. EU AI Act uses 10²⁵ FLOPs for GPAI obligations; US executive orders have referenced 10²⁶ FLOPs. Roughly: GPT-4 class is around 10²⁴–10²⁵ FLOPs; the next generation is above these thresholds.

capability signal.definition: Any observable indicator that AI capabilities have meaningfully advanced — a new benchmark result, a flagship model release, an agent completing a hard long-horizon task, a lab disclosing a major training run. Used to track whether the scaling curve is holding and what the frontier looks like versus the state-of-the-art a quarter ago.

benchmark.definition: A standardized test used to compare AI model capabilities — MMLU, HumanEval, GPQA, SWE-bench, etc. Important caveat: labs know the benchmarks and may (intentionally or not) overfit to them. A benchmark result is a signal, not ground truth. Watch for new 'hard' benchmarks that haven't been saturated yet.

inference-time compute.definition: Using extra computation at inference (not training) to improve outputs — e.g., chain-of-thought reasoning, search trees, self-consistency sampling. OpenAI's o1/o3 and DeepSeek-R1 pushed this approach. The key question: does it compound with training-time scaling, or substitute for it?

open weights.definition: A model whose weights (the learned parameters) are publicly released, allowing anyone to run, fine-tune, or modify it. Meta's Llama series is the leading example. Distinct from 'open source' (which implies reproducible training). Open-weights models compress the capability gap between frontier labs and everyone else.

flops.definition: Floating-point operations. The standard unit for measuring AI training compute. A GPT-3-scale training run is ~3×10²³ FLOPs; GPT-4 class is estimated around 10²⁴–10²⁵ FLOPs; frontier 2025-era models are around 10²⁶ FLOPs. Used in regulation as the threshold to define 'frontier.'

huawei ascend.definition: Huawei's domestic AI accelerator chip series (Ascend 910B/910C). Built on SMIC's 7nm-class process, it's China's main attempt at an H100 substitute. Performance is reportedly 60-70% of H100 at comparable tasks; limited by HBM availability and yield issues. The most watched signal for China's AI compute independence.

deepseek.definition: Chinese AI lab that shocked the AI world in early 2025 with DeepSeek-R1 — a frontier-class reasoning model trained at a fraction of US lab costs, then released open-weights. Demonstrated that efficient training can partially compensate for compute disadvantage under export controls. Key capability signal for China's AI trajectory.

em.definition: Emerging Markets — the bucket macro investors use for non-developed economies (China, India, Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia, South Africa, etc.). 'EM debt' is sovereign and corporate bonds from these countries; 'EM equity' is their stock markets. EM is sensitive to dollar strength (debts often USD-denominated), commodity prices (many are exporters), and global risk appetite — when DXY rises or US rates spike, EM tends to bleed.

monetary stimulus.definition: Central-bank actions to ease financial conditions and encourage borrowing/spending — cutting policy rates, asset purchases (QE), liquidity facilities. Works in normal cycles by lowering the cost of credit. Famously *fails* in a balance-sheet recession (Japan post-1990, China post-2021): when households and firms are paying down debt, no rate is low enough to make them borrow. Then the lever that actually works is fiscal stimulus aimed at household demand, not more cheap credit.

ig.definition: Investment Grade. The top tier of corporate credit quality — bonds rated BBB-/Baa3 or higher by S&P/Moody's. Pension funds, insurers, and most passive bond ETFs are restricted to IG paper, so a downgrade from IG to high-yield ('fallen angel') forces mechanical selling. The IG/HY boundary is the most consequential single line in the credit market.

ig corporate debt index.definition: A benchmark basket of investment-grade corporate bonds (e.g., Bloomberg US Corporate IG Index) that passive funds and ETFs like LQD track. Issuer weights are set by market value of debt outstanding, so the biggest borrowers automatically become the biggest index positions — which is how hyperscaler bond issuance silently concentrates passive-bond-fund exposure to AI capex.

pjm auction shortfall.definition: PJM is the largest US grid operator (Mid-Atlantic + Midwest). Each year it runs a 'capacity auction' to procure enough generation to meet projected peak demand plus a reliability margin. A shortfall means cleared capacity came in below that target — in Dec 2025, by 6,623 MW. Clearing prices spike when this happens, and the gap signals that new generation isn't being added fast enough to absorb data-center load growth.

ferc colocation.definition: Federal Energy Regulatory Commission rules on whether a data center can sit directly next to a power plant and take electricity 'behind-the-meter' (bypassing the grid). FERC's Dec-18-2025 order forced PJM to publish a colocation framework — three transmission service options and reformed behind-the-meter generation rules. The decision unlocks deals like Talen–AWS (Susquehanna nuclear) and is the regulatory hinge for hyperscalers buying baseload power directly from generators instead of waiting in 8-year grid interconnection queues.

loi.definition: Letter of Intent. A non-binding agreement signaling commercial intent to do a deal — used as a placeholder before a final binding contract. Common for capex-heavy deals (data centers, PPAs, chip supply) where the parties want to publicly lock in alignment while the terms are still being negotiated. An LOI is real signal (legal/financial teams agreed to put it on paper) but not yet a contract.

lqd.definition: iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF — the canonical retail-accessible way to own a basket of US investment-grade corporate bonds. ~$30B in assets, holds ~2,500 IG bonds weighted by market value of debt outstanding. ~4% of LQD is hyperscaler paper (META, GOOG, AMZN, ORCL), and *that share rises mechanically* every time a hyperscaler issues new debt — passive bond exposure is silently long AI capex.

agg.definition: iShares Core US Aggregate Bond ETF (and the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index it tracks) — the standard 'total US bond market' benchmark. Holds Treasuries, agency MBS, and IG corporates in market-cap weights. Roughly 25–30% corporate credit, of which a slice is hyperscaler debt. If you own AGG or BND (Vanguard's equivalent), you have indirect hyperscaler-bond exposure.

slip risk.definition: The probability that a scheduled product launch, shipment, or capacity ramp gets pushed later than the company guided. Stock-market shorthand for 'deadlines tend to move right.' Sits alongside yield risk (does it work at spec) and demand risk (will customers still want it) as the three core schedule risks for any physical-product company. For NVDA pre-W20, slip risk on Vera Rubin was the dominant variable being priced; for hyperscaler data centers, the Omdia 'half of US builds delayed or canceled' finding is slip risk crystallizing at the buildout layer.

capex curve.definition: The trajectory of total AI infrastructure spending by hyperscalers over time — ~$200B in 2024, ~$430B in 2025, ~$725B in 2026. The central object of the AI bubble debate: rising means the buildout is intact; flat means saturation; falling is the regime change. Distinct from the *capability-per-dollar curve* (efficiency gains within each GPU generation) — the two are separate levers on whether AI keeps improving.

capability per dollar.definition: How much AI capability (intelligence, useful work, tokens served at quality) you get per dollar of compute spent. Has risen with each GPU generation (V100→A100→H100→B200→Rubin). The 'efficiency lever' on the AI scaling story — improving capability-per-dollar lets labs keep pushing the frontier without proportionally climbing the capex curve. The bear case is the inverse: rising capex but flat capability-per-dollar means diminishing returns on scaling laws are showing up.

hbm4.definition: Fourth generation of High-Bandwidth Memory. Targeting ~2.0–2.5 TB/s per stack (vs HBM3e's ~1.2–1.3 TB/s) with more stacks per package, ~75% better power efficiency, and pin speeds >11 Gb/s. Sole suppliers: SK Hynix (lead), Samsung, Micron. The single biggest lever behind Vera Rubin's ~10× lower inference cost claim — inference is memory-bandwidth-bound, so doubling HBM bandwidth roughly doubles tokens-per-second-per-GPU.

kv cache.definition: Key-Value cache. During LLM inference, each token's attention keys and values are stored in GPU memory so subsequent tokens don't recompute them. Grows linearly with sequence length × in-flight requests, so it dominates HBM usage at scale. More HBM capacity per GPU → more KV cache resident → more requests batched simultaneously and longer contexts servable without paging. The hardware substrate that makes continuous batching scale.

continuous batching.definition: Inference scheduling technique (also called 'in-flight batching' or 'iteration-level batching') where new requests are added to a running batch as old ones finish, instead of waiting for a fixed batch to complete together. Standard in vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang. Hugely improves GPU utilization for production LLM serving where requests arrive asynchronously. A software technique, but its effectiveness is gated by KV cache memory.

prefill decode.definition: The two phases of LLM inference. **Prefill** = process the prompt and build initial KV cache (compute-bound, parallel across tokens). **Decode** = generate output tokens one at a time, autoregressively (memory-bandwidth-bound, sequential). They have opposite bottlenecks, so running them on the same GPU wastes one side's resources. 'Disaggregated serving' routes prefill and decode to different hardware — Rubin CPX is Nvidia's first chip designed specifically for the prefill phase, a major lever in Rubin's inference cost story.

rubin cpx.definition: A separate Nvidia chip in the Rubin family designed specifically for the *prefill* phase of LLM inference (compute-heavy, long-context processing). Pairs with standard Rubin GPUs that handle *decode* (memory-bandwidth-bound token generation). Hardware-native support for disaggregated serving — previously done in software (DistServe, Splitwise). Most important for long-context and agentic workloads where prefill cost dominates.

vera rubin.definition: Nvidia's GPU generation after Blackwell, named after the astronomer. Mass production ramp Q3 2026, July delivery to top US customers (de-risked May 15, 2026). Headline claims: ~10× lower inference cost per token, 75% fewer GPUs to train an equivalent model vs Blackwell. Achieved via HBM4, FP4/FP6 second gen, Rubin CPX (prefill chip), NVL576 fabric, and improved perf/watt. The platform that the late-2026 / early-2027 frontier models (Claude 5, GPT-6, Gemini 4) will train on.

fp4.definition: 4-bit floating-point number format. Quantizing model weights and activations from FP16/BF16 (16-bit) to FP4 cuts memory and roughly doubles math throughput per chip, typically with minor quality loss for inference. Blackwell introduced hardware FP4 support; Rubin extends it. The standard precision tier for production LLM inference in 2026.

moe.definition: Mixture-of-Experts. An LLM architecture where the model has many 'expert' subnetworks but only routes each token to a few of them at a time. Lets you scale total parameters (capacity) without proportionally scaling per-token compute. Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-5, and Gemini are MoE. Expert parallelism (distributing experts across GPUs) benefits hugely from large low-latency interconnect domains — the case for NVL72 / NVL576 fabrics.

nvlink.definition: Nvidia's proprietary high-bandwidth GPU-to-GPU interconnect, much faster than PCIe or InfiniBand. The NVLink 'domain' is the cluster of GPUs that can talk at NVLink speed: Blackwell GB200 NVL72 = 72 GPUs; Rubin Ultra NVL576 = 576 GPUs. Large NVLink domains are essential for tensor and expert parallelism — they let a single training or inference job span many GPUs without interconnect being the bottleneck.

s-1.definition: The registration document a company files with the SEC to go public. It's the first time audited financials — revenue, losses, cash burn, major contracts — become public, which is why an S-1 turns a private company's economics from rumor into disclosure. A 'confidential' S-1 lets the company file privately first; details go public ~15 days before the roadshow.

roadshow.definition: The pre-IPO marketing tour where a company and its underwriters pitch institutional investors to build the order book and set the offer price. The roadshow date effectively starts the clock on a public listing; SpaceX's was set for June 8, 2026.

run rate.definition: An annualized figure extrapolated from a recent shorter period — e.g. ~$2B of monthly revenue stated as a ~$25B annual run rate. Useful for fast-growing companies where trailing-twelve-month numbers understate current scale, but it assumes the recent pace holds.

memory wall.definition: The growing gap between how fast a chip can compute and how fast it can be fed data from memory. Modern AI accelerators can do far more math per second than they can stream weights/activations in, so the expensive compute units sit idle waiting on memory — making workloads 'memory-bandwidth-bound' rather than compute-bound. This is why HBM bandwidth, on-chip cache, and interconnect matter as much as raw FLOPs.

data movement.definition: The cost (time + energy) of getting data to where computation happens, across a hierarchy of distances: on-chip (logic↔SRAM cache), chip↔HBM memory, and chip↔chip (NVLink/interconnect). For AI chips, data movement — not transistor count — is increasingly the binding constraint, because the compute is starved for data (see memory wall). Optimizing it means shorter paths, more cache, faster memory, and tighter packaging.

logicfolding.definition: Huawei's brand name (paired with its 'Tau Scaling Law' framing) for an architectural strategy announced May 2026: chase performance via 3D layout and shorter on-chip data paths rather than shrinking transistors — the lever China can't pull without EUV lithography. The bet is that since leading-edge AI chips are bottlenecked on data movement anyway, attacking that axis can claw back usable performance despite a transistor-size disadvantage. A claim, not yet demonstrated in shipped silicon.

tau scaling law.definition: Huawei's proposed framing (May 2026) that chip performance should be measured by how fast data moves within the chip (τ = time-to-move-data) rather than by transistor feature size. It's a narrative reframing of the performance leaderboard onto an axis where US export controls (EUV) give China less of a handicap. Marketing/strategy positioning, not an established physical law.

fiscal year.definition: A company's 12-month accounting year, which often doesn't align with the calendar year. NVDA's fiscal year ends late January (FY27 = Feb 2026–Jan 2027); Microsoft ends in June; Apple ends in late September. Always check the fiscal-year convention before comparing 'Q1' across companies — NVDA's Q1 FY27 (Feb–Apr 2026) is a different time period than Microsoft's Q1 FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026).

quarterly guide.definition: The company's forecast of next quarter's revenue (and sometimes margin, opex, capex), provided on the current quarter's earnings call. Wall Street trades the *delta between guide and consensus* more than the actual print. NVDA's Q2 FY27 guide of $91B is the dollar revenue management expects in the 3-month May–July 2026 window — not year-to-date. A guide is non-binding but companies that miss their own guide tend to get punished severely.
